passage:
Hiring note. Varun, team manager, after Thursday's interviews.
What I saw: Of eight candidates, the panel rated highest the three who matched the profile of our last star hire, Siddhant: top-tier college, crisp English, a startup internship. Nitin said of one, "He's another Siddhant, we can't miss him." Nobody asked that candidate the design question we had planned. The candidate from a regional college who solved the design problem best, and explained a real bug she had fixed, got "not polished" written in the margin.
What I did: I proposed a scoring sheet for the next round. The same five questions for everyone, each scored separately with examples, before anyone discusses overall fit. The panel agreed to try it.

qa.q: What was written in the margin for the candidate from a regional college?
qa.a: "Not polished" was written in the margin.

qa.q: Why did Nitin feel sure about the candidate called another Siddhant?
qa.a: Nitin felt confident and eager because the candidate matched the profile of their last star hire, so the resemblance felt like evidence of future success and the design question seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: Why does Varun's scoring sheet help?
qa.a: Asking everyone the same five questions and scoring each one with examples before discussing fit makes the panel judge what candidates actually show, not how much they resemble past hires.

qa.q: How might the candidate from the regional college feel if shown the margin note?
qa.a: She would likely feel unfairly judged, since she solved the design problem best and explained a real bug, yet was marked down for style.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing a panel favouring candidates who resemble a past star hire and proposing structured scoring on actual evidence.

passage:
Tuesday night, Gangtok
Long day of interviews for the hotel front desk. I noticed something I didn't like. Varun and the other panellists kept lighting up for anyone who reminded them of Karma, our best receptionist last year: tall, hotel-school, smooth English. One candidate barely answered the complaint scenario, but Varun said, "Very Karma-like, great presence." A woman from a village near Namchi handled the angry-guest role-play beautifully, in Nepali and then English, and got marked "average fit". I kept thinking: we're hiring a shadow of Karma, not the best person. Tomorrow I'll ask the panel to score each skill separately, with an example for each, before anyone says "fit". My wife says I'll annoy everyone. Probably.
Pema

qa.q: What mark did the woman from near Namchi get?
qa.a: She got marked "average fit".

qa.q: What was Pema worried about after the interviews?
qa.a: Pema felt the panel was favouring people who resembled Karma rather than those who did the job best, and worried they were hiring a shadow of a past success.

qa.q: What is Pema planning, and why could it work?
qa.a: Pema plans to have each skill scored separately with an example before anyone mentions fit, so strong performance, like the angry-guest role-play, counts more than resemblance.

qa.q: How might Varun react to the new scoring plan?
qa.a: Varun may feel a bit defensive at first, since presence felt like a real signal, but might accept it once the scores show who handled the tasks best.

grounding: Shows a hiring panellist noticing panellists favouring candidates who look like a past success and planning skill-by-skill scoring instead.

passage: At the block office in Bhawanipatna, three people sat on the panel to hire teachers for the new village learning centres: Hemant, the programme manager, and two senior coordinators, Sarika and Irawati. Last year's best teacher, Sudhir, had come from the town college and spoke smooth English. By the fourth interview Hemant noticed a pattern. Whenever a candidate mentioned the town college or answered in English, Sarika's pen started moving fast. When a young woman from a nearby village answered in Kui and Odia, describing how she had run an evening class for twenty children, Irawati said, "Nice, but not like Sudhir." At tea, Hemant took a sheet of paper from his bag. "Can we agree what we're actually hiring for? Teaching children in their language, patience, attendance records. Let's each score those, one to five, before we talk." Sarika frowned, then nodded. The village woman's scores came out highest.

qa.q: Where did last year's best teacher, Sudhir, come from?
qa.a: Sudhir had come from the town college.

qa.q: What does Hemant seem to think as he watches Sarika's pen move fast?
qa.a: He seems uneasy, noticing that candidates who look and sound like Sudhir are being favoured whether or not they fit the actual job.

qa.q: What did Hemant propose at tea, and why did it work better?
qa.a: He proposed that each panellist score the real job needs, such as teaching in the children's language, patience and attendance, before discussing. That made them judge each person on evidence.

qa.q: How might the young woman from the nearby village have felt if the panel had not changed its method?
qa.a: She might have felt her real teaching experience counted for nothing because she did not resemble last year's star.

grounding: A programme manager in a small town notices a hiring panel favouring candidates like an earlier star, and proposes structured scoring.

passage: The bakery chain in Toronto was hiring four shift leads, and Tariq, the new operations manager, sat on the panel with Rosa from HR and a regional manager. Their best shift lead ever, Kevin, had been a college athlete, a tall, loud man full of energy. By Wednesday afternoon Tariq could see it: every candidate who played team sports got warm smiles and extra time. A quiet woman who had run a busy night shift at a hospital cafeteria for three years got twelve minutes and a polite goodbye. "She just didn't have that Kevin spark," Rosa said. Tariq didn't argue about spark. Instead he opened a laptop. "What if we list five things a shift lead actually does, like handling complaints, scheduling, stock, safety, training, and score each person on examples?" Rosa hesitated. "That's more work." "It is. But it's fairer." They re-scored the week's candidates that evening.

qa.q: How long had the quiet woman run a busy night shift at a hospital cafeteria?
qa.a: For three years.

qa.q: What does Rosa's comment about "that Kevin spark" suggest about Rosa's thinking?
qa.a: Rosa seems to feel warm and comfortable with candidates who resemble Kevin, using him as the picture of a good shift lead, even if the job needs other skills.

qa.q: Which choice by Tariq helped the panel judge more fairly?
qa.a: Instead of arguing about spark, he listed five real tasks of a shift lead and asked the panel to score each person on examples.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel about the extra work of structured scoring?
qa.a: Rosa may feel a bit reluctant or defensive at first, but seeing the re-scored candidates side by side could help Rosa notice what had been missed.

grounding: A manager abroad notices his panel favouring candidates who resemble a past star, and proposes scoring everyone on real job tasks.

passage: The hiring panel at the hospital's IT department had seen six candidates by lunch. Abhinav was excited about the fourth. "He's another Rakesh. Same college, same cricket-club style, even the same laugh. Rakesh turned out brilliant." The third panellist agreed. Hemant, running a panel for the first time, looked at his notes. The fifth candidate, a woman from a small polytechnic, had solved the database problem fastest and explained it most clearly. Nobody had mentioned her. "Can I suggest something?" Hemant said. "Let's each score all six on the same four points: the problem, the explanation, the teamwork answer and learning. Out of five. Before we talk." Abhinav grumbled but filled in the sheet. When the scores were added, the fifth candidate was first, and Rakesh's lookalike was fourth.

qa.q: How many candidates had the panel seen by lunch?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Hemant suggest scoring before talking?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that the panel was drawn to a candidate who resembled Rakesh while nobody mentioned the candidate who had solved the problem best.

qa.q: Why does scoring all six on the same four points help?
qa.a: It makes each panellist judge every candidate on the same evidence before excitement about a lookalike can sway the room.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when the scores are added?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel surprised and a little embarrassed that the lookalike he liked came fourth.

grounding: A young manager notices his panel favouring a candidate who resembles a past success and proposes scoring everyone on the same points.

passage:
Subject: Proposal for next week's interview panels
Hi Sabina,
After sitting on three panels for the analyst roles, I want to flag something. Last year's best hire came from Pune and played football, and since then we keep rating candidates higher when they share those things. On Tuesday one candidate got "strong fit" from two panellists mainly because "he reminds us of Kunal." Another candidate, who answered the case question best, got "not sure about culture."
I'd like us to try a simple structure: the same five questions for everyone, each scored from 1 to 5 against written examples of weak and strong answers, scored alone before any discussion. We can compare the results after a month.
Happy to draft the sheet by Friday.
Thanks,
Yash

qa.q: Why did one candidate get "strong fit" on Tuesday?
qa.a: Mainly because two panellists said he reminded them of Kunal.

qa.q: What worried Yash after the three panels?
qa.a: Yash felt worried that panellists were rating candidates on resemblance to last year's best hire rather than on their answers.

qa.q: What does Yash propose, and why could it work?
qa.a: The same five questions for everyone, each scored alone against written examples before discussion, so answers count more than resemblance.

qa.q: How might the candidate who answered the case question best be affected by the current way of judging?
qa.a: That candidate could be turned down for "culture" despite the best answer, losing a chance through no fault of their own.

grounding: A young manager emails HR after noticing panels favour candidates who resemble a past hire, proposing structured scoring.

passage: Ganga, the story I tell new managers is from my first hiring panel, when I was the only man under thirty in the room. We were choosing trainee chefs for the hotel kitchen. The head chef kept lighting up at candidates who had trained where he had, spoke like him, even stood like him. "This one has the look," he'd say. A young woman from a small catering college cooked the best omelette of the day, and he said, "Not the type." I was scared to contradict him. So I didn't argue about her. I said, "Chef, can we taste blind for the next round? Numbers on the plates, scores on a sheet, names after?" He shrugged and agreed. She came first. Dhruv, the nervous junior, got to feel useful that day.

qa.q: What did the young woman from the catering college cook?
qa.a: The best omelette of the day.

qa.q: How was Dhruv feeling about speaking up?
qa.a: Dhruv was scared to contradict the head chef, so chose a neutral method instead of arguing about one candidate.

qa.q: Why did the blind tasting work better than arguing?
qa.a: It judged every candidate on the food itself, so looks and training background could not sway the scores.

qa.q: How might the head chef see the blind-tasting result?
qa.a: He may be surprised that the candidate he called not the type came first, and it could make him question his instinct for the look.

grounding: A young man on a hiring panel notices the head chef favouring candidates like himself and proposes blind, scored tasting.

passage: I've been hiring manager at a small design studio in Pune for two years, and last month I noticed something about my co-panellist, Sudha. We were interviewing for junior designers. Sudha lit up at every candidate from the same design school our best designer came from. "She reminds me of Pooja," she said twice. She rated them high before looking at their portfolios. A candidate from a small college in Nagpur brought an excellent portfolio. Sudha said, "Hmm, not really our type." I felt uneasy. We were judging resemblance, not work. After the interviews, I proposed a simple scoring sheet: portfolio, problem-solving task, and interview answers, each scored separately, before we discussed. Sudha agreed, a bit stiffly. With the sheet, the Nagpur candidate came out top. I'm Darshan, and as a man who once got hired for 'looking right,' I should have noticed sooner.

qa.a: "Hmm, not really our type."

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling as Sudha rated candidates by resemblance?
qa.a: Darshan felt uneasy, realising they were judging people by how much they looked like past successes rather than their actual work.

qa.q: Why does structured scoring help, as Darshan proposed?
qa.a: Scoring portfolio, task and answers separately before discussing makes each candidate judged on evidence, not on resemblance to someone else.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about the scoring sheet?
qa.a: Sudha seems a bit stiff and perhaps defensive, but agrees to try it.

grounding: It shows a hiring manager who notices a panel favouring candidates who resemble earlier successes and proposes structured scoring based on evidence.

A Monday in February. On the interview panel for sales trainees in Bengaluru, Yash noticed that Rehana, his co-panellist, smiled most at tall, confident men from engineering colleges, just like their current top salesman. "He's a natural," she said after five minutes with one of them.

That Thursday. The candidates she liked had weaker answers to the customer scenario. A quiet woman from a commerce college had the best solution but got a low mark from Rehana. "She's not the sales type." Yash felt his jaw tighten. He wasn't sure how to raise it without sounding like an accusation.

The next Monday. Yash brought a scoring sheet to the panel: scenario answer, product knowledge, and a role-play, each scored alone, before any discussion. "It'll make us fairer," he said. Rehana shrugged but used it. The quiet woman scored highest. Rehana looked at the sheet for a long time.

qa.q: Who did Rehana say was 'a natural'?
qa.a: One of the tall, confident men from engineering colleges.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Rehana dismissed the best solution?
qa.a: Yash felt frustrated, his jaw tightening, and unsure how to raise it without sounding like an accusation.

qa.q: What did Yash's scoring sheet change, and why?
qa.a: It made each candidate scored on answers, knowledge and role-play separately, so the quiet woman's real ability showed instead of resemblance to the top salesman.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel looking at the final scores?
qa.a: Rehana may feel surprised and thoughtful, seeing that her first impressions didn't match the evidence.

grounding: It shows a manager who notices a panel favouring candidates who look like earlier successes and brings in structured scoring, over a week.

passage: Afreen, you're joining your first interview panel next week? Let me tell you what I saw as a young man of twenty-five, a junior manager in a bank in Kolkata. Our branch head liked candidates who looked like him: Bengali, from his college, played cricket. He'd say, "This one has spark," in the first minute. I noticed that a quiet young woman from Siliguri with top scores was rejected because she "didn't fit." It bothered me for weeks. I was nervous, being junior. But I went to him with a simple idea: let's each score candidates on the same questions, separately, then compare. He grumbled but agreed to try it for one round. That round, two people from outside his usual type came out on top, and both became excellent officers. So, Afreen, use a scoring sheet. It's how Pranav learned to see people, not types.

qa.q: How did young Pranav feel about the Siliguri candidate's rejection?

qa.a: Pranav's decision to suggest separate scoring on the same questions, which let candidates outside the usual type be judged on evidence.

passage:
Twenty candidates in one day, a power cut at noon, and the generator fumes drifting into the interview room in Indore. Darshan was tired. So were the other two panel members.

By four o'clock he noticed a pattern. Pooja kept saying, "This one reminds me of Karthik," the best engineer they'd hired last year. Those candidates got high scores. A woman from a small college who'd answered every technical question well got "not quite our type". A man who spoke softly got "lacks presence".

Darshan felt uneasy. They weren't judging answers. They were judging resemblance.

During the tea break, he pulled out a sheet. "For the last six, can we try something? Same five questions for everyone. Each of us scores each answer from one to five, separately, before discussing."

Pooja frowned. "That's slow."

"It's fairer. And we'll know why we picked someone."

They tried it. The woman from the small college came out on top.

qa.a: Twenty candidates in one day.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling by four o'clock?
qa.a: Darshan felt tired and uneasy, noticing the panel was scoring people by resemblance rather than by their answers.

qa.q: What did Darshan propose, and why is it better?
qa.a: Darshan proposed the same five questions for all and separate scores of one to five before discussion, so people are judged on evidence, not resemblance.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when the woman from the small college came out on top?
qa.a: Pooja might feel surprised and a little uncomfortable, realising the comparisons to Karthik had been steering her.

passage:
Farhan had been sitting on hiring panels at the Mumbai bank for two years before he noticed it.

Every candidate who had studied at the same college as the branch head, played cricket, and spoke with a certain confidence got through. The ones who looked or sounded different, a woman with a strong Bihari accent, a man in a wheelchair, a shy man who stammered at first, rarely did, however well they answered.

Then his colleague Amandeep mentioned during lunch, "That last candidate reminded me so much of our top performer." Farhan realised that was the whole method.

He went to the branch head with a proposal: every panel would use the same questions, scored separately on a written sheet, with notes explaining each score. No discussion until all scores were in.

In the next hiring round, four of the eight new joiners came from backgrounds the old panels had quietly passed over.

qa.q: How many of the eight new joiners came from backgrounds the old panels had passed over?
qa.a: Four of the eight new joiners.

qa.q: What did Farhan realise after Amandeep's comment at lunch?
qa.a: Farhan felt troubled, realising that judging by resemblance to past successes was the panel's whole method.

qa.q: Why was Farhan's structured scoring a good fix?
qa.a: Using the same questions and separate written scores forced the panel to judge each candidate's actual answers instead of how much they resembled past hires.

qa.q: How might the candidate with the Bihari accent see a structured interview?
qa.a: That candidate would likely feel judged more fairly, on answers rather than accent.

grounding: A manager notices panels favouring candidates who resemble earlier successes and introduces structured scoring.

passage:
I'm Baljeet, and last month I sat on my first interview panel as a new manager. By the fourth candidate, I noticed something uncomfortable.
My two senior colleagues kept lighting up at candidates who looked like our star analyst from last year: same college, same crisp way of talking, even the same kind of watch. "Very much like Vikram," one said, and gave top marks. A candidate named Vidya, who had solved the case study best, got middling scores. "Not quite our type," the other colleague said.
I checked my own notes and realised I'd been doing it too, at least a little.
So after the round, I suggested we try structured scoring: the same four questions for everyone, each marked against a clear rubric, before any discussion. My colleagues grumbled, but agreed to try.
When we re-scored with the rubric, Vidya came first. We hired her. Two months on, she is the best analyst on the team.

qa.q: Who solved the case study best?
qa.a: Vidya had solved the case study best.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when noticing the panel's pattern?
qa.a: Baljeet felt uncomfortable, especially on realising the same pull had shaped Baljeet's own notes a little.

qa.q: What did Baljeet propose, and why does it help?
qa.a: Structured scoring, the same questions with a clear rubric before discussion, so candidates are judged on actual evidence instead of resemblance to past successes.

qa.q: How might Vidya have been affected if the panel hadn't re-scored?
qa.a: Vidya, the strongest candidate, would likely have been passed over for not being "our type", and the team would have lost its best analyst.
